title: Jind Kaur's death, 1863
hookLine: she dies in London, and her son takes her ashes toward India
last: SHE TOLD HIM WHO HE WAS.

lines: A QUEEN WHO WON'T SEE LAHORE.
HOW DO YOU TAKE HER HOME?
cards: In a rented house in Kensington, with London's carriages passing in the street, a queen of the Punjab is dying.
She has been a regent, a prisoner, a fugitive across the hills to Nepal, and, at the end, a mother living near her son. She will not see Lahore again.
And when she dies, her son faces a question no English gentleman is trained for: how do you take your mother home?

teach.b: Jind Kaur lived near Duleep Singh in London after their meeting in Calcutta.

teach.h: A DEATH FAR FROM THE PUNJAB.
teach.b: Her health was poor and her sight was failing, but she kept telling him about the Punjab, and the histories suggest the stories took hold. She died in London, far from the land she had ruled as regent.

Sikh custom is to cremate the body. In Victorian London that was not a simple thing to arrange, and her son wanted her rites done in India, not in England. So he took his mother's body by sea toward India.
But he was not permitted to take her into the Punjab.
She was cremated on the banks of the Godavari river at Nasik, far to the south of the land she had known, and a small memorial was built there.
Her ashes, tradition says, were later moved to Lahore and laid near her husband's memorial, though that came long afterward.
In the Alahniyan, the songs of mourning by Guru Nanak in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that whoever has come must rise and go, and that this world is a passing show.
At a Sikh funeral the hymns are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are given to flowing water.
A son who had been raised far from all of it did what he could to carry his mother home, and got as close as he was allowed.

how: At a Sikh funeral, hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are placed in flowing water; Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur in histories and gatherings about the end of the kingdom.

games.q: you're Duleep Singh. your mother has died in London, and you want her rites done at home. what happens, as the histories tell it?
o: you take her by sea toward India, but aren't allowed into the Punjab.
games.why: she was cremated by the Godavari at Nasik, as close to home as he was allowed.

practice: Bring to mind a mother, your own, someone else's, or a woman who mothered you without the name, and picture her hands doing something ordinary: stirring a pot, folding clothes, holding a cup.
If she has died, let the memory rest in you without needing to do anything with it; if she's living, simply hold her in your mind. If you pray, let Waheguru be your word as you breathe.
